prompt.context: Our client is Caesars, one of the largest gaming and resort companies in the world. Penn and Teller have been the headlining show at the Rio Hotel since 2001, and they are currently the longest-running headlining show in Vegas history. Caesars, who owns the Rio Hotel where the duo performs in the 1,500 seat P&T Theater, is wondering if their act has become stale. Penn & Teller's annual contract is about to expire, and before Caesars has a meeting with the duo, they have asked our company's advice on whether or not to re-sign the act for another year.
prompt.question: Should Caesars re-sign Penn and Teller for another year? Caesars cares solely about bottom line profitability.

clarifying_info.a: As one of the largest entertainment companies on the Strip and around the world, Caesars solely cares about the company's bottom line profitability.

clarifying_info.q: How long is a contract for Penn & Teller?
clarifying_info.a: As is the Vegas standard, all contracts are for a one-year time period.

clarifying_info.q: Why does Caesars think the show is stale?
clarifying_info.a: The show has plateaued with no change in bottom line profitability in the past five years.
Caesars' biggest competitor is MGM Resorts, which also operates about 33% of the Strip. P&T compete against a whole bevy of nighttime entertainment, such as other shows, nightclubs, and gaming.

clarifying_info.q: How many seats does the theater have?
Are all the seats the same price?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are three categories. There are 300 Category A seats (best seats in the house), 800 Category B seats, and 400 Category C seats (balcony, or in the back of the theater).

clarifying_info.q: Do the seats always sell out?
clarifying_info.a: No. On average, 100% of the A, 80% of the B, and 50% of the C are sold.
Category A costs $120, B costs $75, C costs $55.

clarifying_info.q: How many shows do P&T perform?
clarifying_info.a: They perform at Vegas' standard 6 shows per week, 40 weeks per year (they have 1 day off per week and three months per year when they work on other endeavors like TV appearances and book deals).
These numbers have been static over the past 5+ years, hence why Caesars thinks the show has become stale.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to putting on the show?
clarifying_info.a: Costs are broken into six main buckets: (1) Both Penn and Teller each make $2,000,000 per year; (2) The Crew (showgirls, ushers) in total costs $2,000 per show; (3) Housekeeping costs $1,000 per week; (4) The Props (the doves, playing cards, etc.) cost $200 per show; (5) Utilities (the lights) cost $52,000 per year; (6) SG&A (box office staff, etc.) costs $15,000 per month.
No, they are only needed the 40 weeks the show is live.
Yes, that is a 12-month per year expense.
These costs have been static over the past 5 years.

framework: 1. Revenue from P&T show — A. Price: types of tickets, price per ticket; B. Volume: capacity, sell-through by ticket type
2. Costs — A. Variable: consumables (props, handbills), labor (cleaning, ushers, stagehands), utilities; B. Fixed: marketing, SG&A, annual contracts, insurance, room fees
3. Impact on other revenue — gambling, dining
4. Alternatives — replacement acts and cost/benefit; alternate use of the space (more casino space, buffet, etc.)

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual revenue from the Penn and Teller show.
questions.guidance: Candidate should break revenue down by seat category, compute per-show revenue, then annualize. Strong candidates note that not all seats sell out and use the correct sell-through rates.

math.setup: Revenue per show = (seats * sell-through * price) summed across all three categories. Annual revenue = revenue per show * shows per week * weeks per year.

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual costs of the Penn and Teller show.
questions.guidance: Candidate should itemize each of the six cost buckets, apply the correct time base (per show vs. per week vs. per month vs. per year), and sum to a total. Key watch-out: housekeeping is only 40 weeks (not 52); SG&A is 12 months.

math.setup: Annualize each cost item using its correct frequency, then sum.

questions.prompt: What is the annual profit and margin of the P&T show?
questions.guidance: Straightforward subtraction and division after completing the revenue and cost calculations.

math.setup: Profit = Revenue - Cost; Margin = Profit / Revenue

questions.prompt: Caesars has the opportunity to switch the P&T show for one featuring the recent winner of America's Got Talent (AGT). The new show would bring in $90,000 in ticket sales per show and cost $3,000,000 per year. Installing the new show requires a one-time upfront investment of $2,400,000. Should Caesars make the switch?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare the incremental annual profit change and calculate the payback period on the upfront investment. Strong candidates flag risks: 4-year payback is long in a competitive market; AGT winners may not have lasting appeal.

math.setup: Calculate incremental annual revenue change, incremental annual cost change, net new annual profit delta, then payback period = upfront cost / annual profit improvement.
steps: Net annual profit change: -$1,200,000 + $1,800,000 = +$600,000 per year
math.answer: The AGT show is $600,000 more profitable per year, but requires a 4-year payback period on the $2,400,000 upfront investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What can Caesars do to make the current P&T show more profitable?

categories.name: Revenue — Ticket Pricing
ideas: Increase ticket prices across one or more categories
Convert some Category B seats to Category A (higher-margin seats)
Convert some Category C seats to Category B

categories.name: Revenue — Volume
ideas: Offer bundle discounts to increase sell-through on C seats
Put on more shows per week
Bundle tickets with dinner, overnight stay, or other activities

categories.name: Revenue — Other
ideas: Retool the concession stand for higher margin
Add a gift shop with P&T-branded souvenirs
Shorten the show so viewers return to gaming sooner (higher-margin activity for Caesars)

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Revisit and renegotiate the contract with Penn and Teller
Review crew labor — check union vs. non-union options to reduce labor costs

recommendation: Option A (Re-sign P&T): Recommend that Caesars re-sign Penn and Teller. The show remains highly profitable, generating $18,000,000 profit (~80% margin) on $22,800,000 in revenues. Although the AGT alternative is incrementally more profitable, the 4-year payback period on the $2,400,000 upfront investment introduces meaningful risk.

Option B (Do not re-sign P&T): Recommend that Caesars does not re-sign Penn and Teller. The show has stagnated with no growth, and the new AGT act is fresher and would generate an additional $600,000 in annual profit once the upfront cost is recouped.
risks: Assumption that Penn and Teller will maintain their popularity if re-signed
Risk that Penn and Teller demand higher salaries at renegotiation, compressing margin
The 4-year payback period for the AGT switch is long in a highly competitive market
No guarantee that an AGT winner has lasting popular appeal beyond the initial excitement
next_steps: If re-signing P&T: explore revenue upside levers — price increases, seat reconfiguration, concessions, bundling — and cost reduction opportunities such as labor renegotiation
If switching to AGT: conduct additional market research on the resilience of AGT-winner appeal; evaluate whether alternative acts offer higher profitability with shorter payback periods
